source.title: Training-free Truthfulness Detection via Value Vectors in LLMs
source.authors: Runheng Liu; Heyan Huang; Xing-Chen Xiao; Zhi-Jing Wu

record.tranche_reason: The study measures truthfulness-related activation patterns in individual MLP value vectors, but does not audit how many neuron poles have a nameable main job, test explanations on held-out activations, or test any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports per-vector truthfulness prediction results and a semantic interpretability analysis. The prediction results do not measure the claim's interpretability estimates. The interpretability analysis concerns selected truthfulness-predictive vectors and uses vocabulary projection and t-SNE, not an audit of poles or tested explanations.
record.test_reason: The study relies on individual MLP value vectors as units carrying content-level signals and reports its own truthfulness-detection method's accuracy. It does not audit how many neurons have a nameable job, does not score explanations against held-out activations, and does not test any version. Its small vocabulary-projection check covers only the selected top vectors, and no share is reported. 'Uses without test' (T4) fits better than 'discusses' (T6), because the method builds on individual value vectors.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a sparse subset of MLP value vectors shows directionally consistent, context-dependent activation differences between truthful and untruthful content. They propose TruthV, which uses these vectors to beat training-free baselines across benchmarks and model sizes from 2B to 13B. They also report that the selected vectors lack surface-level vocabulary-projection semantics, and speculate that the vectors encode abstract or distributed properties or that GLU architectures reduce direct interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The study ranks individual MLP value-vector activations for truthfulness prediction and probes selected vectors with vocabulary projection and t-SNE; it does not generate and test neuron-job explanations or estimate an interpretable-pole share.

fits_no_version.finding: The top truthfulness-predictive MLP value vectors in Llama-2, Gemma-2, Llama-3.2 and Qwen3 show no surface-level semantic alignment under vocabulary projection and no clear t-SNE clustering. The authors suggest they belong to a non-interpretable subset or encode abstract or distributed properties.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLP value vectors selected for predicting content truthfulness lack interpretable vocabulary-projection semantics in modern GLU-based LLMs.

record.problems: The semantic interpretability findings are qualitative, with no reported per-model or per-dataset results or uncertainty estimates; the paper notes that vocabulary projection may miss abstract or distributed properties.
record.rows_left_out: Truthfulness-prediction accuracy results, benchmark comparisons, and activation-distribution analyses were left out because they do not measure neuron-job interpretability or any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit of neuron poles.
There is no share of interpretable neurons for any model. The models are 2B–13B dense only.
No vision models and no canonical polysemantic examples.
There is no measured comparison of architecture or tools. The authors only speculate that GLU MLPs may reduce interpretability under vocabulary projection.
No explanations are written from activating examples and then tested.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Geva et al.'s figure that about 50% of GPT-2 value vectors match no concept. That is a cited result, not this study's own, so it should not be a row. The GLU-architecture remark loosely relates to V4 but is speculation without data.

versions.untested_parts: Does not estimate the share of Qwen3-32B neuron poles with one or two jobs or that are not understood.
Evaluates models at several sizes, but does not audit interpretable-job shares across models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or trillion-parameter scales.
Does not analyze InceptionV1 or the cat-and-car example, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not compare architectures, regularization, or tools as causes of interpretability rates, and does not evaluate InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Does not construct attribution graphs or assess whether neurons suffice as circuit units without a replacement model.
Does not test natural-language explanations against activation behavior on examples they were not written from.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: Selected highest-accuracy value vectors across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Gemma-2-2B-it, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Qwen3-4B
rows.stage_stated: chat, it, and instruct variants; training method not stated
rows.operation_detail: Projected the value vector selected for highest accuracy on each dataset into vocabulary space and inspected its top-10 tokens for semantic alignment.

conditions.value: highest-accuracy value vector for each dataset

rows.measure: Surface-level semantic alignment of selected value vectors with truthfulness
rows.value: No evidence of surface-level semantic alignment between top-scoring tokens and truthfulness
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Semantic interpretability of truthfulness-related value vectors
rows.note: The paper describes the finding generally across its selected vectors; it gives no per-model or per-dataset breakdown. It also notes that vectors could encode abstract or distributed properties, so this result does not establish whether they have a nameable main job.
rows.check: This is a qualitative vocabulary-projection check of one selected top-accuracy vector per dataset. It reports no count and no interpretable share, and it tests only alignment with 'truthfulness' tokens, not whether the neuron has some other main job. It cannot bear on V1, V2 or V6.

rows.measure: Clustering of selected truthfulness-related value vectors
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Semantic interpretability of truthfulness-related value vectors
rows.note: The paper gives this as a general statement without a per-model or per-dataset breakdown. Lack of clustering does not determine whether individual vectors have a nameable main job.
rows.check: t-SNE clustering of selected vectors measures whether they form a shared subspace, not whether each neuron is interpretable. It bears on no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
